opening_summary: Thirty-two terms for the Unreal Editor, for someone who already knows Godot, from the viewport and panels to Play In Editor, Blueprints, collision and settings. The exact name tells you, or an AI coding agent, which part to use.
opening_description: 32 Unreal Editor terms: panels, play, Blueprints.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Someone coming from Godot often says the Outliner lists every asset in the project. It does not. The Outliner lists the Actors placed in the open level. The assets on disk live in the Content Browser. The Unreal Editor is full of look-alike pairs like that one. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown.
idea.text:
The Outliner lists
every asset in the project.
idea.replacementWords: every Actor in the open level

beats.narration: This table is the map, thirty-two terms in four groups. The first group, look and move, holds the Level Viewport, perspective and orthographic, view modes, right-mouse fly, the Content Browser, the Content Drawer, the Outliner and the Details panel. It covers where you look, and where things are listed.

The second group is place and play. The Place Actors panel, World Settings, the Main toolbar, Play In Editor, Simulate, Eject, PIE changes discarded, where PIE is short for Play In Editor, and the Output Log. These say how you add things, run them, and read what happened.

The third group is what a level holds. Actor and Component, Blueprint class, Level and Levels window, dot u asset and dot u map, object type and response, and collision preset. These are the objects and the files behind the panels.

The fourth group is editors and settings. The Blueprint Editor, Event Graph, Construction Script, Material Editor, Niagara, the Animation editors, Project Settings, Editor Preferences, Plugins, and Build and Package. These are the tools you open from assets, and the switches around them.

This is a drawing of the Unreal Editor, not a screenshot, and panels can be moved, so your own layout may differ. The Level Viewport, lit in red, is the main window onto the level. You see the Actors there, the objects placed in the level, select one, and move it. Here the Cube is selected. For example, in a small platformer you would select a platform in the Level Viewport and drag it under a jump.

The Content Browser, lit along the bottom, is where you browse, import and organize every asset in the project, the files on disk. Here it holds a door Blueprint, a cube mesh and a wood material. Drag the door into the viewport and the Outliner lists three Actors. The Content Browser lists assets, and the Outliner lists Actors. For example, when you import a coin sound for your game, it turns up in the Content Browser, ready to use.

The Outliner, lit at the top right, is a tree of every Actor in the open level. You can search it and sort it into folders. Select a name there, here the door, and the same Actor is selected in the viewport. For example, in a level crowded with coins and spikes, you would type coin into the Outliner's search to find the coins, rather than hunting for them in the viewport.

The Details panel shows the properties and the Components of the selected Actor, and lets you edit them. Here the door's Location X is changed from zero to three hundred, and the door moves right. In this drawing that is ninety pixels, at an illustrative zero point three pixels per unit. For example, select a moving platform in your level, and the Details panel is where you type its new position.

The Main toolbar runs along the top. It holds Save, mode switching, adding content, and the Play and Stop controls. Here Play is pressed, the button reads Playing, and the game runs inside the editor until Stop ends it. For example, after you place a new jump pad in your level, you press Play on the Main toolbar to try it, and Stop to go back to editing.

Two drawings of the same cube, from two cameras. Perspective shows depth, so far things look smaller. Orthographic drops depth, so parallel edges stay parallel and equal. Measured here, the short edge divided by the long edge is zero point six seven in perspective, and one point zero zero in orthographic. Perspective is the default view. For example, to line up a row of platforms at exactly one height, you would switch to an orthographic Side view.

Now three view modes. A view mode is a way of drawing the same scene, such as Lit, Unlit and Wireframe. Lit shades each face by the light, here from a grey of one hundred twenty to two hundred forty. Unlit gives every face the same grey. Wireframe draws only the twelve edges. The scene itself never changes. For example, if a dark corner of your level hides a coin, switch to Unlit to see that the coin is really there.

A top view of the viewport camera flying through a room. Right-mouse fly means holding the right mouse button and pressing W, A, S and D to move the viewport camera, while the mouse turns it. In this drawing it goes forward for two seconds, turns, goes forward again, moves sideways, turns, and goes forward once more. For example, you would fly through a long level this way to look at a ledge before putting a coin on it.

A viewport, with a Content Drawer button underneath. The Content Drawer is a Content Browser that rises from the bottom left, covers the viewport, and hides again when you click away. Here it opens and then hides. A docked Content Browser stays open, and the drawer pops up and goes away. For example, while laying out a level, you open the Content Drawer, drag a spike asset into the viewport, and the drawer tucks itself away again.

The Place Actors panel is a palette of Actor types, such as Cube, Sphere and Cylinder, that you drag into the level. Here a Cube is dragged out of the Basic tab and lands on the floor, and the Outliner count goes from two to three. For example, to block out the first room of your game, you drag cubes from the Place Actors panel to make the floor and walls, and a light from the Lights tab.

World Settings holds values for the open level as a whole, such as its Game Mode and Kill Z. An Actor that falls below Kill Z is removed. In this example Kill Z is minus one thousand, and a ball falling a thousand units at nine hundred eighty units per second squared takes one point four three seconds, then is destroyed. For example, Kill Z is what removes a player who falls off the last platform of your level.

An Outliner on the left, and Details on the right. An Actor is an object you can place in a level. A Component is a piece of behaviour or data attached to it. The door Actor is selected, and Details lists its three Components, a root, a door mesh and a box trigger. For example, a coin in your game would be one Actor, with a mesh Component for its look and a trigger Component that notices the player.

A Blueprint class is Unreal's reusable object template, built visually or in code. Each placed copy follows the class default, unless that copy overrides it. Here the class default Open Angle is set to one hundred ten. Copies one and three show it, and copy two keeps its own forty-five. The class is the template, and each copy is an Actor. For example, one enemy Blueprint class could set the patrol speed for every enemy you place, with one slow guard overriding it.

A toolbar with Play, Simulate, Stop and Eject, over a viewport and an Output Log. Play In Editor, or PIE, means running the game inside the editor. You are the player, and the keys go to the game, not the editor. Editor Python scripts are not available inside it. In this simulated run the player walks to x equals five hundred fifty pixels. For example, you press Play to run your platformer in the editor and steer the character over the gaps yourself.

Simulate runs the level's logic and physics with no player, and you keep the editor camera. Here a ball falls and bounces with nobody playing. Play In Editor makes you the player, and Simulate leaves the level running on its own. For example, to see whether a stack of crates in your level topples by itself, you press Simulate instead of Play, and keep your camera free to look around.

Eject works while you are playing. It releases the player so you can fly the camera and select Actors, and play goes on. Here the player stays put, and the camera moves off to look over the level. For example, an enemy in your game gets stuck against a wall during a test. You press Eject, fly over, and select the enemy to look at its values while the game keeps running.

A chart of the door's X value over six seconds. PIE changes discarded is the rule that edits made to Actors during play are thrown away when you stop, while edits made before play stay. Here the door is set to three hundred during play, and at Stop it drops back to zero. For example, you tune a jump pad's strength during a test until it feels right, and at Stop the value is gone, so set it again before pressing Play.

The Output Log is a window of messages from the editor and the game, with warnings and errors marked. Print String text appears there too. Here there are three messages, a plain one, a warning that no key was found, and an error in red, the door has no mesh. For example, if a coin never adds to the score, you print a line when the coin is touched, and look for that line in the Output Log.

A Levels window beside a viewport of dots, one dot for each Actor. A level is one playable space, saved as a map file. The Levels window lists the levels in the world, and an eye switches each one on or off. In this made-up example the levels hold twelve, five and forty Actors, fifty-seven in all, and Rooms off leaves seventeen. For example, you could switch off the Rooms level while you adjust the lights of a large map.

Dot u asset and dot u map are Unreal's binary files, one for assets and one for levels. A text tool cannot open them or merge them. Here the same change, an open angle from ninety to one hundred ten, shows as one readable line in a Godot scene file, and only as binary files differ in the map file. For example, an AI coding agent can read the text scene file of your level, but not a dot u map of the same level.

Now two people edit the same file. In the text file one edits line twelve and the other line forty, and git merges both, two of two kept. In the binary map file git cannot combine them, so one edit is kept, one of two. Source control also locks a binary file while one person has it checked out, and the editor has its own diff tool. For example, two teammates on one Unreal level would take turns on the map file.

This is a different window, the Blueprint Editor. It opens when you open a Blueprint class, and it is separate from the level window. Its parts are Components, My Blueprint, a Viewport, the Event Graph and Details, with Compile, Save and Play along the top. Here the door Blueprint shows its mesh, its trigger, and a variable named Has Key. For example, you would open an enemy Blueprint in the Blueprint Editor to add a variable for its health.

The Event Graph is the node-and-wire view of a Blueprint, where execution wires set the order the nodes run, and it runs when play events fire. Here Event BeginPlay runs first, then a Branch tests Has Key. If true, Open Door runs. If false, Print String runs. Three nodes either way. For example, a pickup's Event Graph could start from its begin overlap event, add one to the score, and then remove the pickup.

The Construction Script is a graph that runs when the Actor is built or changed in the editor, before play. Here a loop adds one fence post for each step of Count. Count changes from three to five in Details, and two posts appear without pressing Play. The Event Graph waits for play, and the Construction Script runs as you edit. For example, a bridge Blueprint could lay down as many planks as its length value asks for, right in the editor.

A small node graph. The Material Editor is a node graph that builds a material, and its result node takes Base Color and more. In this simulated example a wood texture is multiplied by a Brightness scalar of zero point five zero, so every colour channel halves, and red goes from one hundred seventy-six to eighty-eight. For example, to make a cave level darker, you could lower one brightness node in the rock material instead of repainting the texture.

Niagara is Unreal's visual-effects system. A system holds emitters, and each emitter is a stack of modules that run in order, top to bottom. Here the sparks emitter's modules light one by one, and the burst module spawns thirty-two particles at once. The Material Editor turns nodes into a colour. Niagara is systems, emitters and modules. For example, when an enemy in your game is defeated, a Niagara system could throw out a single burst of sparks where it stood.

The Animation editors are the windows you open from animation assets, a Sequence, a Montage or an Animation Blueprint. Here a sword swing Sequence runs thirty frames at thirty frames per second. A notify marks frames twelve to seventeen, a window of six frames, or zero point two seconds, and the sword's hitbox is live only inside it. For example, if a sword hit landed before the blade reached the enemy, you would move that notify later in the Sequence.

A lane with a pickup, a player and a wall, and a table of pairs. Each object has an object type, and a response to every other type, Block, Overlap or Ignore. A pair gets the weaker of its two answers, so Block needs both sides to block. The player and the wall block, and the other two pairs overlap. For example, a spike hazard set to Overlap the player, with overlap events enabled on both, lets the player into it and fires the event that ends the run.

A Collision preset is a named bundle of responses, such as BlockAll, OverlapAll or NoCollision, so one choice sets many responses at once. Here the pickup's preset becomes NoCollision. All its responses read Ignore, and the player and pickup pair now reads Ignore too. For example, you would give the outer walls of your level the BlockAll preset, so they answer Block to every type, without setting each response by hand.

A shared project folder, with you and a teammate below it. Project Settings are settings saved with the project and shared by everyone who opens it. Here the Default Map is set to Arena, and the teammate sees Arena too. Project Settings go with the project, and Editor Preferences stay on your machine. For example, if you set the first level of your game as the Default Map, every teammate who opens the project gets that same setting.

Editor Preferences are settings for you and your own copy of the editor, not saved with the project. Here you switch your theme to Dark, and your teammate's editor stays Light. One of two copies changed. For example, you might switch to a dark theme while you build your platformer at night, and your teammate never sees it, because that choice is an Editor Preference.

Plugins are add-on modules you switch on or off for each project, and most need an editor restart. Here the Python Editor Script plugin is switched on, one of three, and the editor asks for a restart. Paper 2D and Unreal MCP, a plugin for the Model Context Protocol, stay off. For example, before an AI coding agent can run an editor Python script on your level, the Python Editor Script plugin has to be switched on.

Build and Package means turning the project into a runnable game. Package Project is the Unreal word for making a build, for one platform. The project's asset and level files go in, a Cook step turns the assets into the form the platform uses, and they are packaged into a game folder. For example, when your platformer is ready for a playtest, you pick a platform and run Package Project to get a game folder the playtester can run.

A table that matches Unreal parts to their nearest Godot parts. The match is close, not exact. First, the Level Viewport matches Godot's 2D and 3D main view. Both are where you see the scene and move things. For example, nudging a platform to the left happens in the Level Viewport in Unreal, and in the 2D view in Godot.

The Outliner matches Godot's Scene dock. Each is a tree of what is in the open scene, which in Unreal is the open level. For example, finding the player among the platforms and coins means looking in the Outliner in Unreal, and in the Scene dock in Godot.

The Content Browser matches Godot's FileSystem dock. Both list every file in the project, whether or not it is placed in a level. For example, a jump sound you add to your game turns up in the Content Browser in Unreal, and in the FileSystem dock in Godot.

The Details panel matches Godot's Inspector. Both show the properties of whatever is selected, and let you change them. For example, changing an enemy's patrol speed by hand means typing a new value into the Details panel in Unreal, or into the Inspector in Godot.

The Output Log matches Godot's Output panel. Both show messages from the editor and the game. For example, a line printed when the player lands a jump appears in the Output panel in Godot, and a Print String in a Blueprint appears in the Output Log in Unreal.

Play In Editor matches Godot's Run Project and Run Scene. Both run the game, and in both, edits made to a live run are lost. For example, a speed you tweak on the player while the game is running is gone when the run stops, in either engine.

A Blueprint class matches a Godot scene, saved as a dot t s c n file. Each is a reusable template of an object, so a Blueprint class is nearer to a scene than to a script. For example, a coin you place many times in a level is one Blueprint class in Unreal, and one coin scene in Godot.

The Material Editor matches Godot's VisualShader editor. Both build a material from nodes, wired together on a graph, instead of from typed code. For example, a glowing outline on a pickup could be built from nodes in the Material Editor in Unreal, or in the VisualShader editor in Godot.

Package Project matches Godot's Export. Both make a build to ship, a game that runs without the editor. That completes the nine pairs. For example, the copy of your platformer that you hand to a playtester comes from Package Project in Unreal, and from Export in Godot.

Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. In Play In Editor you are the player, and your keys move the player. In Simulate there is no player. Physics runs, nobody plays, and you keep the editor camera.
The Content Browser lists assets on disk. There is one door Blueprint asset, and it stays one however many you place. The Outliner lists the Actors in the level, here three placed copies of it.
Project Settings are saved with the project and shared, so a change reaches the teammate. Editor Preferences are yours alone and not in the project, so a change stops at your machine.
Package, on its own, is a saved asset, one dot u asset file. Package Project is the whole game as a build. Many files go in, and one game comes out.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it, beside a chart of what it does. See the game from the side becomes, switch the viewport from Perspective to Orthographic, Side view. The edge ratio goes from zero point six seven to one point zero zero.

Test the door while I edit becomes, press Play, change Door X, press Stop, and it goes back to its saved value. Before Play the door is at zero, during Play at three hundred, and after Stop at zero again.

Find what went wrong becomes, open the Output Log, filter to Error, and read the first line. Of forty log lines in this seeded example, twenty-five are plain, twelve are warnings and three are errors. That leaves three lines to read.

Make the pickup not block me becomes, set the pickup's response to the player to Overlap, and enable overlap events on both Actors. The player and pickup pair goes from Block to Overlap, and the player and wall pair stays Block.
Check what changed in that Blueprint becomes, use the editor's diff tool, because git diff only says binary files differ. Git shows two changed lines in a text scene file, and zero in a binary asset.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change made in the Unreal Editor. First, am I in the level editor, or in a running PIE window?
Second, did I change it while playing? Play changes are discarded at Stop, so make the edit again with the game stopped.
Third, did I save the level and the changed assets? An edit that is not saved is not yet part of the project.
Fourth, is this a Project Setting, shared with everyone who opens the project, or only my Editor Preference, which stays on my machine?
Fifth, is the file text, or is it a dot u asset or dot u map file that an AI coding agent cannot read? If it is binary, the review happens in the editor, by you.
Sixth, do both objects answer Block, or Overlap, for the pair? Then say it exactly. Not try it, but press Play, then Stop, and read the Output Log.

recap_lines: The Outliner lists Actors in the level, and the Content Browser lists assets.
A Blueprint class is the template, and each placed copy is an Actor.
Play In Editor makes you the player, and Simulate runs with no player.
Edits made to Actors during play are thrown away when you press Stop.
Dot u asset and dot u map files are binary, so text tools cannot merge them.
A collision pair gets the weaker of its two responses.

your_turn.command: Give me short cases from building a small game in Unreal, one at a time, and ask which part of the editor or which rule each case needs. Use Outliner, Content Browser, Details panel, Play In Editor, Simulate, Eject, Blueprint class, Event Graph, Construction Script and collision preset. I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Wait for my answer before you give yours.
checks: Check: every case comes from building a game, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you used the exact term and ruled out its look-alike.

deck_problems: Slide 9 (Material Editor, Niagara and the Animation editors), step 2: the Niagara particles spawn at the bottom edge of the viewport box and fall out of it (renderEditors, k 2: cy = 420 + v[1]*ts*0.6 + 0.5*300*ts*ts). At the end of the step they are scattered over the caption and the TELL THESE APART box, while the viewport, which says 'particles alive: 32', is empty.
Slide 8 step 2: the Event Graph definition says 'white execution wires set the order', but the wires drawn are red and black; no white wire appears.
Slide 6 step 5: the tab reads 'filter: Warning, Error', yet the Output Log still lists the plain line 'Door opened', which that filter would hide.

Slide 6 step 4: the chart has two play markers, a bare play triangle at 1 s where the pink play zone starts and a 'Play' label at 3 s under the ramp where the door is edited. The 'Play' label reads as if play began at 3 s.
Slide 6 step 3: the caption says 'player stays where it was', but the player is drawn near x 330, not where step 1 left it ('x = 550 px').
Slide 3 step 1: the perspective cube spills below its box and its lower edge crosses the 'short edge ÷ long edge' label, covering the word 'long'.
Slide 13 step 1: the Simulate ball comes to rest on the caption 'physics runs, nobody plays' and hides the word 'nobody'. No floor is drawn for it.
Slide 4 step 1: the Content Drawer bar under the viewport overlaps the 'TELL THESE APART' heading.
Slide 2 versus slide 5: SM_Cube is an asset in the Content Browser on slide 2 (the placed Actor is called 'Cube' in the Outliner), but on slide 5 SM_Cube is listed in the Outliner as a placed Actor.

Slide 14 step 4: the exact instruction says only 'enable overlap events', not on both Actors. Chapter 4 says both Actors need Generate Overlap Events, and slide 10's caption says overlap needs both sides.
Slide 11 step 4 names a pipeline box 'Package' (Cook, Package, Game folder), while slide 13 pair 4 defines Package as one saved asset file. The two senses of the word sit side by side without a note.

Sources and notes disagree in small ways: slide 7's note cites Chapters 1, 4 and 5 for the binary quote while its source line lists Chapters 0, 1 and 5; slide 11's note says the plugins come from Chapters 0, 1 and 4 while its source line says Chapters 0 and 4; the title slide's note says 'Deck 15 of the topic order' for deck 25.
